Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn The film You Don’t Belong Here , directed by Florin Șerban, will premiere at this year’s Locarno Film Festival, where it has been selected in the International Competition. The film explores the complex relationship between a father and his son. It follows a physician as he learns the police suspect his teenage son of murdering an old Romani man, then discovers his son has a secret life. The cast includes Adrian Văncică, Teodor Butănescu, Alex Conovaru, Cristina Richter, Janir Izdrăilă, and Cosmin Dominte. The world premiere will take place on August 9 at Forum - Spazio Cinema. Following the screening, members of the film's crew will take part in a Q&A session. Additional screenings are scheduled for August 10 and August 11. You Don’t Belong Here has also been selected in the main competition of the Sarajevo Film Festival. Florin Şerban's debut feature, If I Want to Whistle, I Whistle , premiered in the competition section of the 2010 Berlinale, where it won the Silver Bear and the Alfred Bauer Prize. Held from August 5-15, 2026, the Locarno Film Festival is one of the world's oldest film festivals. Founded in 1946 in the aftermath of the Second World War, it has built its reputation on championing freedom of expression, independent cinema, and auteur filmmaking. https://www.dw.com/en/kazakhstan-parliam.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JGpK Kazakhs are voting in an election that was triggered by the adoption of a new constitution earlier this year Image: Pavel Mikheyev/REUTERS Advertisement Kazakhstan's ruling party comforably won an election for the country's new, single-chamber parliament on Sunday, according to exit polls. State television shared three exit polls giving the Adilet party between 70% and 72% of the vote. The vote comes after a new constitution approved in March did away with the Senate to create a new unicameral Kurultai — a reference to the medieval councils of the region's nomadic past. Backers of the new body say it will give parliament more say in decision making, critics argue it will only cement the power of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev . The 73-year-old took the reins from authoritarian Nursultan Nazarbayev — who himself ruled the country for 30 years after the collapse of the Soviet Union — in 2019. The constitutional reform also opens the door for President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev to stay in power Image: Turar Kazangapov/REUTERS The pro-presidential Adilet party was expected to win an overwhelming majority in Sunday's vote, while exit polls showed four smaller parties loyal to Tokayev also won seats in the new parliament. Seven state-approved parties have been allowed to field candidates for the 145-seat parliament while genuine opposition parties have been banned. The election took place amid soaring inflation (which is hovering around 10.2%) and rising taxes, fueling concerns for the government — and particularly Tokayev — of a repeat of January 2022 cost of living unrest that left 238 protesters and police dead . Inequality, corruption led to Kazakhstan unrest To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Press crackdown and financial strain color Kazakhstan's election Beyond financial strain, Sunday's vote also took place against the background of crackdowns on press freedom , with numerous reporters under house arrest and official criminal cases being brought against 10 independent journalists and bloggers. Tokayev, a former Soviet official and Kazakh diplomat who worked at the UN, touted his reforms and justified the many changes he has initiated — including the introduction of the new constitution — as necessary in a fast-changing world. "Without a doubt, these elections will be remembered as perhaps the most interesting in our country's history," said Tokayev on Friday. "Amid unprecedented geopolitical tensions and mounting global challenges, we must firmly and consistently implement our strategy to transform Kazakhstan into a truly developed state," he added. Tokayev has sought to maintain a delicate balance between Moscow — with their shared Soviet ties — and the West since sanctions were imposed on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine . Resource-rich and strategically located Kazakhstan also has ties to China and the European Union . Although Tokayev has said that he has no plans of staying in power beyond his current term, the constitutional reform that 87% of voters backed this March effectively reset term limits for the office — making him eligible to run for another seven-year stint in 2029 should he change his mind. How can Kazakhstan navigate ties with Russia and China? https://www.dw.com/en/ard-deutschlandtre.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NdWm SPD leader and Vice-Chancellor Lars Klingbeil (l) and CDU leader and Chancellor Friedrich Merz are feeling the mounting pressure on their government Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Ahead of October 3, which marks the reunification of West and East Germany in 1990, pollster infratest dimap asked 1303 eligible voters to assess their personal situation. Twenty percent of those identifying as East Germans , but 44% see personal advantages. Only a quarter said reunification had no major impact on them personally. More than half of West German respondents said reunification had no major impact on their personal lives. The remaining half is split: 19% said reunification had a positive impact, while 18% said it had a negative one. Germany held three state elections in September, two of them in eastern states. They were seen as a test of nationwide voter sentiment. The results were particularly devastating for the center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz . In Saxony-Anhalt and the city-state of Berlin, where it had been in government, the CDU dropped by 10% compared to the previous election and lost its hold on power. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania , the party even failed to cross the 5% threshold for representation in parliament. This has never happened before in Germany's history. Merz under pressure: CDU lawmaker on election setbacks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Chancellor Merz wants to remain in office Merz has long been unpopular and has seen his support fall even further in the aftermath of the elections. The coalition he leads, comprised of the CDU, the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), is unpopular. Only one in 10 respondents in the survey said they were satisfied with the federal government's work and the chancellor's performance, a historic low. Only 40% of CDU supporters say they are still satisfied with Merz. Far-right AfD in the lead nationwide The Alternative for Germany (AfD), which the domestic intelligence agency has classified as, in part, far-right extremist, continues to benefit from the voter dissatisfaction with the centrist parties. If a general election were held now, the CDU/CSU alliance would win only 20% of the vote. That is one of the lowest figures in the party's history and a far cry from the 43.8% it won in the first election after reunification in 1990. The SPD polls at only 13%. This means that the ruling parties together would not even win one-third of the vote and would lose their majority in parliament. The AfD would remain the strongest political force. It has been polling steadily at 27% nationwide. The environmentalist Greens are up slightly, reaching 16%, while the socialist Left Party has dropped by the same margin, landing at 11%. With this result, it would be a Herculean task to form a majority in the national parliament. AI, Russia and Donald Trump's policies The overall situation in Germany gives only one in eight people cause for optimism, while nearly nine in 10 express concern. Voters for the AfD and the Left Party are particularly worried. Two-thirds of respondents said they're worried that humans could lose control over artificial intelligence , and just as many are worried about the consequences of US President Donald Trump 's policies for Germany. Six in 10 expressed concern about climate change, and just over half said they are worried that Russia could attack other countries in Europe . About one in two respondents fear they will not be able to maintain their standard of living in the future. A similar number are concerned about immigration to Germany . By far the biggest source of concern for Germans, however, is that political parties cannot find common answers to key political issues. Why Germany's political center is losing ground To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Social reforms must be fair Germany is a rapidly aging country. Fewer working people must support an ever-increasing number of retirees. The aging society also strains the health care system. Since 2015, the number of people in need of long-term care has risen from about 2.8 million to about 6.5 million — and the trend continues to rise. According to the ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, only one in six eligible voters believes that the federal government will succeed in making the social security systems sustainable for the future . Not all respondents said they are willing to dig into their own pockets: Voters who tend to support left-leaning parties would be more likely to accept higher social security contributions than benefit cuts. Among AfD and CDU/CSU voters, the opposite is true. Three-quarters of respondents view the government's proposed reform measures as contradictory. They complain about an ever-increasing burden, even though the government had promised relief. What Germans young and old think about the pension system To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Sixty-one percent say that cuts should be scaled according to individual financial capacity, even if this would place a heavier burden on some people. One in two would be more willing to accept cuts if the necessity were explained in a way that made sense. The message to policymakers is clear: reforms require explanation and social balance; otherwise, they lose acceptance. The welfare state and the health care system are regarded as key achievements in Germany. When asked what works particularly well in Germany compared to other countries, survey respondents most often cited social benefits and medical care. Education, schools, vocational training and universities came in last place. Energy policy is seen as a problem High energy prices continue to burden citizens and the German economy. The ongoing crisis in the Persian Gulf is driving oil prices even higher . This is impacting fuel and electricity prices in Germany. Respondents to the ARD Deutschlandtrend survey found that the government is not doing enough to address high energy prices . Three-quarters of them said the government's efforts are insufficient. A "Tankrabatt" (fuel discount) has again come into effect on October 1: Through the end of the year, the federal government is reducing the energy tax on gasoline and diesel by about 17 eurocents ($0.19) per liter. A similar discount was already in place from early May through the end of June. That cost the government €3.4 billion. Some of that money ended up in the pockets of oil companies and gas station operators because they did not pass on the full discount. Experts view the measure critically. Added to this is the fact that fossil fuels are being made cheaper despite shortages, which is controversial from a climate policy perspective. The new fuel discount has received only a lukewarm reception among the public; half of those surveyed in the ARD Deutschlandtrend poll believe it is the wrong approach. This article was originally written in German. http://www.greekherald.com/news/27931987.text: Polish diplomatic security chief critically injured in fall from embassy window RT.com 21 Sep 2026, 05:23 GMT+10 The senior Foreign Ministry official reportedly plunged from the third floor while attending a private gathering in Slovenia A senior Polish Foreign Ministry official has been critically injured after falling from a third-floor window at a building adjoining the country's diplomatic mission in Slovenia, local media have reported. The incident occurred at around 3am on September 13 but only came to light several days later. The man was identified by Polish outlets as the head of the Foreign Ministry's Diplomatic Security Bureau, which oversees the security of ministry facilities in Poland and the country's diplomatic missions abroad. He has remained in critical condition in a Slovenian hospital since the fall. According to Polish news portal Zero.pl, the official was attending a private party with several other people when he fell. The other participants were also reportedly off duty. "He was on leave. It was his private time. He was in an apartment adjacent to the diplomatic mission. That is where the accident occurred," ministry spokesman Maciej Wewior told Niezalezna.pl. Despite being on vacation, the official had reportedly collected a diplomatic package and was expected to deliver it onward without a formal assignment. Slovenian police were reportedly not permitted to enter the diplomatic premises or inspect the scene because the Polish mission did not grant its consent. The Polish side said its own investigators would examine the site and investigate the circumstances, TV Slovenija journalist Marko Saksida said. Polish Deputy Sejm Speaker Krzysztof Bosak described the circumstances as suspicious and called for a thorough investigation. "Security-related positions in the Foreign Ministry are often filled by people from the security services. If someone falls from a window at a diplomatic mission and it turns out that he was on vacation and carrying some kind of package, the case is no longer merely mysterious but very, very suspicious," he said. The mission is headed by charge d'affaires Leszek Soczewica, whom Polish media have described as a close friend and associate of Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski. In December 2022, Poland faced another high-profile security controversy when national police chief Jaroslaw Szymczyk was hospitalized after a grenade launcher presented to him as a gift by Ukrainian officials exploded inside police headquarters in Warsaw. Szymczyk said he had been assured that the weapon was unloaded, but security experts criticized his decision to bring military equipment into Poland and keep it in his office. Abbott outlines law enforcement, fentanyl strategy during roundtable in San Antonio KSAT Investigates Texas Rangers believe Camp Mystic leaders ‘recklessly caused’ 27 flood deaths, warrants show Search warrants seek digital records from Camp Mystic owners, family members and employees Daniela Ibarra , Investigative Reporter Bill Taylor , Special Projects Producer Zaria Oates , Reporter John Paul Barajas , Anchor/Reporter Henry Keller , Multimedia Brand Manager Jarryd Luna , Photojournalist Emilio Sanchez , Photojournalist Myra Arthur , Anchor/Reporter Ken Huizar , Logistics Coordinator Landon Lowe , Executive Producer Brian Collister , Executive Reporter Published: September 22, 2026 at 7:28 PM Updated: September 22, 2026 at 10:22 PM SAN ANTONIO – Texas Rangers believe Camp Mystic leaders “recklessly caused the death” of the 25 campers and two counselors who died during the July 4, 2025 floods, according to search warrants obtained by KSAT on Tuesday. Manslaughter, criminally negligent homicide, abandoning or endangering a child, injury to a child, and deadly conduct, are some of the crimes the warrants accuse camp leaders of committing. “These offenses were committed against child campers -- including both deceased victims and surviving campers of the flood event-- under an operator’s duty of care,” Texas Ranger investigator Brant Johnston wrote in the documents. The warrants would allow Texas Rangers to search electronic records to help investigators figure out what camp leaders and employees knew and did before, during, and after the deadly flood. The 14 warrants are for: Richard “Dick” Eastland Willetta “Tweety” Eastland Edward Eastland Britt Eastland Richard Eastland Jr. Mary Liz Eastland Catie Eastland Glenn Juenke, nightwatchman Rachel Farhoudi, senior counselor Lauren Bass, photographer Jane Charpentier, office assistant Katarzyna Kruk, seasonal worker From Poland Kalina Krol, seasonal worker From Poland Joanna Schwarz, seasonal worker From Poland The New York Times was the first to report on the warrants, which were signed last week. Back in the spring, the Texas Rangers told KSAT they’re assisting the Department of State Health Services (DSHS) in the investigation into Camp Mystic. At the time, Camp Mystic planned to reopen for the 2026 summer camp season, records show. That decision was later scrapped. According to the affidavits, several members of the Eastland family declined to be interviewed by investigators. The documents reveal new details about what happened during the deadly flooding, which also swept away longtime camp owner Dick Eastland. Dick Eastland’s watch data shows he “was submerged in over twenty feet of water” just before 4 a.m on July 4, 2025, according to the court records. His son, Richard Eastland Jr., woke up early that morning. Records show he had trouble falling asleep after his wife texted him to let him know that their rental home was flooded, but that she was safe. He started to work on his computer but realized the internet was out. “Richard looked at his phone, which warned of dangerous flash flooding, but he was not concerned,” stated the document. No one has been criminally charged at this time. Our team is reading through more than 600 pages of court records. We will be updating this story with the details of what we’ve learned.
